newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists yield on elections.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists yield on elections.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists, bowing to 30 days of mass anti-government rallies and strikes, agreed on Tuesday to hold early national elections in April.
A joint statement after crisis talks between the Socialists and opposition parties said they had agreed President Petar Stoyanov "should set early general elections in the second 10 days of April".
Tens of thousands of anti-government demonstrators went wild in central Sofia, dancing, singing and carrying Stoyanov aloft through the streets after he brokered the deal.

The Socialists agreed to elections just hours before their seven-day mandate to form a new cabinet expired. Opposition groups intensified protests in recent days to pile on pressure for the Socialists, the ex-communists, to quit.
The Socialists, elected to a four-year term in 1994, have been savaged for the crumbling economy, with inflation at 50 percent a month and the lev plummeting.

"I do not promise you that you will be richer or you will live better, I promise you that under the next government I will be honest and you will be master of your lives" opposition leader Ivan Kostov told 50,000 jubilant supporters in Sofia.
He must win the April election first but Stoyanov, a UDF candidate, won a landslide victory over the Socialists in November, reflecting the depth of popular dissatisfaction with the government.

Supporters of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) have barricaded road and rail links throughout Bulgaria for a week. Workers have staged strikes in almost every sector, bringing the country to a standstill.
Students have erected barricades and blocked the streets of Sofia for five days and have won the hearts of many residents with their enthusiasm and festive street theatre.

Kostov told a chanting throng: "I would like to thank our president, who managed to take control of this difficult situation, and all the people in the streets, and all those who went on strike for us, and especially the students without whose enthusiasm we wouldn't have gone so far."
The Socialists have overseen a caretaker government since December when prime minister Zhan Videnov quit after Stoyanov's election win and in the face of criticism of his handling of the economy.
The Socialists received a mandate to form a government last week and had until midnight to present their new cabinet.
Under the agreement, they returned the mandate and now each opposition party will do the same. Stoyanov will then appoint an interim government which will serve until the election.
Kostov said he had feared the situation in the Balkan state had become so serious that it could have turned violent.

The UDF called on all demonstrators around the country to lift their blockades and stop their protests, although the UDF plans a final mass victory rally at Alexander Nevski Orthodox cathedral on Wednesday.
